Once the gene has been fully transcribed, the newly created RNA strand is then released from the DNA template.Transcription begins at the promoter region, where the RNA polymerase binds to the DNA template strand. The promoter is located upstream of the gene to be transcribed, which means that it comes before the gene on the DNA template strand. The RNA polymerase attaches itself to the promoter region and scans down the template strand in search of the start site of the gene to be transcribed.Once the RNA polymerase finds the start site of the gene, it starts to synthesise the new RNA molecule. During this process, the RNA polymerase moves away from the DNA template strand to create a new RNA strand. At the same time, the DNA strand acts as a template that provides the code for the new RNA strand.The RNA polymerase continues to move down the template strand until it reaches the transcription terminator sequence, which signals the end of the gene. Transcription ends when the RNA polymerase reaches the stop codon (UGA, UAG, or UAA) on the template strand. The newly formed RNA molecule is then cut off from the DNA template strand. These proteins are essential for the growth and development of organisms. Transcription is a crucial step in the process of protein production. Nuchal translucency is measured between 11.0 – 13.6 weeks, Quadruple test or combined test measurements should be taken after this time (14 weeks) as the nuchal translucency can be difficult to measure before then. Nuchal translucency is a measurement of the area at the back of the foetal head where the spine and neck are visible using ultrasound. The thickness of this area is measured. If the area is thicker than normal this could indicate downs syndrome. The quadruple test looks for abnormalities in four different substances in the mother's body. These are alpha fetoprotein (AFP), human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG), urea and inhibin A. Low levels of all these substances are associated with Down's syndrome. The combined test looks for abnormalities in two different substances mother's body. These are pregnancy associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A) and human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG). Low levels of both of these substances are associated with Down's syndrome. There are also non-invasive prenatal tests that look directly for chromosomal abnormalities in the foetus. They analyse foetal DNA found in the mother's blood and they are available privately but not on the NHS. There are two types of diagnostic tests that can confirm whether a baby has Down's syndrome or not. These are amniocentesis and chorionic villus sampling (CVS). This is usually carried out at around 15 weeks of pregnancy. Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) involves removing a sample of cells from the placenta (this is called the chorion) between 11 weeks and 13 weeks and 6 days of pregnancy.  It is important to note that although screening tests are useful they cannot give a definite diagnosis of Down’s syndrome.
